utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Romano.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness is Xhevahire Syla, but we still don't have a ruling on the admissibility under the 92 bis. And I also point to the Court that this witness also requested to be entirely 92 bis'd, meaning without cross-examination. She will give evidence about the deportation in Djakovica area and also the destruction of the old historic quarter in Djakovica, and that evidence has already been entered by other witnesses, Hasan Pruthi, Andras Riedlmayer. And also for the Meja deportation, there was the evidence given by Merita Dedaj, the witness. So before the witness comes in, the Prosecution requests ask direction under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: She has asked that she be not cross-examined, has she?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No, she is part -- this witness is part of a letter that we sent to the Court, asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: -- around seven or eight witnesses to be treated this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got that. But she's here now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: She's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I thought you said the witness requested to be entirely 92 bis'd.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Sorry. If I said that, that's my mistake; the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Prosecution. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit the statement, but the witness must be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While she's been collected, let me deal with one matter while it's in my mind, which also deals with Rule 92 bis. In fact, she's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Judge Robinson reminds me that a point was made, Ms. Romano, about the time that you take. Could you try and restrict it to five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you, please. But bearing in mind the interpreters. I'm sorry. If you choose to cut out a bit, we have got your summary here, and of course we've had the chance of reading the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No. The summary is extensive, but I do not intend to read out the entire -- and I have already managed to cut it down. Examined by Ms. Romano:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you please state your full name to the Court.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Xhevahire Syla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: I was born on the 13th of February, 1968.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember giving two statements to the Office of the Prosecutor, dated the 2nd of May, 1999, and 5 of October, 2001?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also remember attending a meeting on 14th of March, 2002 in Djakovica, where you attended this meeting in the presence of a presiding officer of this Tribunal, and you had the opportunity to confirm that the contents of your statement are correct and true?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, you also made an addendum to your statement. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you arrived here, Witness, you had again the opportunity to review your statement, and you made a couple of revisions. In the first statement dated 2nd of May, page 2, paragraph 3 states the following: "Later, some commanders of the VJ explained to the villagers that the houses in our village had been hit by mistake. They said that they had been targeting the positions of the KLA in the village of Smoljica." The sentence is incorrect; that's what you said. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not speak to any VJ commander. That's true?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this information was gleaned from other villagers who had spoken to a member of the KLA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: With these corrections, the Prosecution submits the statements into evidence under the 92 bis Rule.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 270 and 270A for the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: This witness was born in Gjakove and lives in Nivokaz, a village about 15 kilometres west of the town. That can be found in Kosovo atlas page 9, map reference F-20. The witness will give evidence of deportation, with associated persecutions, from Gjakove town and villages in the municipality during 1998 and 1999. The witness also gives evidence in relation to the Meja massacre. On the evening of the 24th March, 1999, the witness was still staying with friends in the Cabrat area of Gjakove town. Early on the 25th March, following NATO bombing, she witnessed police armed with incendiary equipment setting houses in the area alight as well as the old market area. The police were also looting property. On 6 April 1999, the police and VJ entered the Cabrat area of Gjakove. The Serb forces shot at the house where the witness was staying and the witness and two other families fled. The witness returned to her own village, but as her own house had been burnt, she stayed at her father's house. On 14 April 1999, mixed Serb forces entered Nivokaz, nine of whom entered in the house where the witness was staying and gave the family five minutes to leave. The witness left on tractor and trailers with many other families. Some of the people in the convoy where the witness joined were assaulted and others told to go to Albania. As the column reached the MUP building in Gjakove, police and soldiers appeared to be in a hurry to ensure that all of the convoy were on tractor trailers and no one was on foot. The convoy continued but was stopped near Bistrazin bridge by police and military who had formed a roadblock. The Serb forces then distanced themselves from the convoy, and thereafter, the column was hit by a NATO bomb. Shortly afterwards, three low-flying aircraft bearing the Serbian flag passed overhead and bombed the convoy seven times, killing 70 to 80 people. On 17 April 1999, residents from Dobros arrived in the village where the witness was staying, stating police had expelled them. The police then arrived and the witness and her family were ordered to go to Albania. She again joined a column of at least 50 other tractors and trailers. In Meja, the column was stopped by Serb mixed forces numbering around 200. The witness saw at least 300 men being taken off the tractors and ordered into a meadow. The men were made to kneel down with their hands behind their heads, guarded by armed police. The police then moved the remaining column on, telling the people to wait in Korenica. 22 of the witness's fellow villagers who were removed from the convoy are still missing, including members of the witness's family. In Korenica, the people in the convoy were robbed by paramilitaries. Both police and paramilitaries escorted the convoy back towards Gjakove and ordered them to continue unescorted to Prizren and at the border. At the border post, VJ soldiers took ID documents from the witness and others in the convoy. She also saw them removing registration plates from vehicles. That's all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement dated the 2nd of May, amongst your details you mention that you're a refugee. Where did you make this statement?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: In Albania.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, at whose suggestion did you make this statement? How did it come about that you gave this statement?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: People came around to take the statements, and I made a declaration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who are these people?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: There was a lawyer, but I don't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A lawyer, an Albanian lawyer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: One was Albanian and one was a foreigner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you give the statement to the best of your recollection or did somebody make suggestions to you as to what kind of statement you're supposed to give?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: I told them only what I had seen and experienced myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you explained to them what we heard now, that NATO and our air force together bombed that convoy of yours. First NATO with one bomb and then our air force with many bombs. That's what you explained to them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't got any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh. So your answer is yes. So now it's clear. You say in your statement that the situation in the village was peaceful all the way up to the 25th of May. Is that correct? Until the 25th of May, that is. For all of two months of the war going on, the situation was peaceful in the village nevertheless; is that right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: There wasn't much going on during the two months, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. A short while ago, we heard a correction that has to do with the assertions that your village was hit by mistake during the fighting between the KLA and the army in the village of Smoljica. What's this all about? Who said that to you? Who told you that it had been so?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: We -- we had to return because we had nowhere else to stay, and we were frightened. And there were a lot of police around the area there, around us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking you about this explanation that your village was hit by mistake when there was fighting between the KLA and the army and the police in the area of the village of Smoljica. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: I don't know anything about Smolica, no, just about Nivokaz. Our house was hit, and a cousin of my husband was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But there was fighting there between the KLA and the army and the police. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: There was not in Nivokaz. There was no KLA in Nivokaz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about Nivokaz. I asked you about the fighting in the area between the KLA and the army and the police. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: There wasn't. At that time, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. How do you then explain what you said in your statement? You say that for a week, people resisted the Serb police and the army of Yugoslavia. And when they ran out of ammunition, they had to flee. Is that what you stated or not? That is to say, when they spent all their ammunition as they were shooting at the army and the police, then they had to run away. That's what it says on page 2 of your statement. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: That is -- that happened in July, not in March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not talking about March at all. In your statement, you refer to the 2nd of May, and you say that for a week, people resisted the Serb police and army, and when they ran out of ammunition, they had to escape. So was there fighting there or was there not fighting there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you look at the dates -- Just a moment. If you look at the dates in the statement, what it says is: "The situation in our village during the last year has been relatively calm until the 25th of May, when at 6.00 a.m., Serbs started shelling our village." And then the witness describes that. Then in the next paragraph, she says: "We continued to live in the village for two months more. Two months after the shelling, the police and VJ tried to capture the village. The village self-organised defence," et cetera. So in fact, she appears to be dealing - in fairness to her - with an event which would have taken place in July.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something that happened after they returned to the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're dealing with 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked whether there had been any fighting, and she says villagers. And now villagers are the KLA. No villagers, no villagers without any arms or anything. They spent all their ammunition and then they escaped. I imagine that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is what she says in her statement, that it was the villagers. But if you're challenging it, it should be put to her. What is alleged is that it was not the villagers who were resisting on this occasion but the KLA. Can you answer that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They only fired at us. They didn't fire during that time. There was a bit of firing at the Serbs but not very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. There was shooting until they used up all their ammunition, from what I can see in your statement, because you say that they escaped when they ran out of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: On the last week, they lived -- in the last week, they came to Nivokaz and stayed there for a time, but we had gone to Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, how many of these people that you mention resisted, as you had put it, the army and the police until they ran out of ammunition? How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: In the village of Nivokaz how many? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you know that they were there and that they were shooting until they ran out of ammunition. So do you have any idea how many were there?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you only know this: As you say, they resisted them until they ran out of ammunition. You don't know how many there were and you don't know who these people were. Actually, you claim that they are villagers, and if you know nothing about this, how come you know that they were villagers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a fair question. She said she doesn't know how many there were, that was all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how long did they resist, as you had put it, until they ran out of ammunition? How long did this go on?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: One week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A week? For a week?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is what she said; a week.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For a week a group of armed men use up all their ammunition. So in a week, one uses up a lot of ammunition. It must have been a lot of people if they managed to resist the army and police for a week. Give me an approximation; how many were there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You've asked that question. She says she doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away is Smoljica from your village? Do you know Smoljica well?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: It's about five kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that Smoljica was a centre where weapons were collected from Albania? In large quantities, at that. Weapons, ammunition, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: No. I've never heard that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never saw that? And did you hear that in April 1998, the largest quantity of weapons until then was brought in from Albania to Smoljica? Did you hear anything about that? Did people talk about it? It's the neighbouring village, after all.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: I wasn't interested in that sort of thing. In the end, I was only interested in saving myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm talking about 1998. Do you know that 370 people with 15 tractors and five trucks brought weapons from Albania? Three hundred seventy men, 15 tractors, five trucks. This was a major event. I imagine you must have known about it. Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: You must ask somebody else, because I don't know. I wasn't there at the event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know who Naim Maloku, Besnik, is? Naim Maloku, nicknamed Besnik.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: I have heard his name, but I don't know what he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hear about the fact that he was the commander, the head of that KLA terrorist group that the KLA organised in Smoljica and the surrounding villages, which includes your village? Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: I never saw him in our -- I never saw him in our village. I can only tell you what I've seen with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me what you heard about him and his activities. Not what you saw but what you heard; tell us that.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about this business. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, there are three statements of yours, and I must admit I wasn't able to link them up. But in your statement of the 5th of September, 2001, and of October, you change your statement and say that they -- the villagers defended the village in July and not in May when they were attacked. What is the truth, the correct one?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell me, what led you to change your statement? Who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've got the statement and I may be wrong about this, but I've got the statement 2nd of May 1999, which I've just read out to you, which refers to the 25th of May and the shelling, and then two months later, the resistance to the Serb forces, which would make it July. So unless I'm wrong about that, there doesn't seem to be any change.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think the difference is quite obvious, but I don't want to waste time, because that's what it says in her statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your statement saying it was in July is correct; is that it? Is that what you claim? Right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your statement of the 2nd of May, you say that the Serbs burnt all the houses. Is that what you said? Right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: 14th of April they burnt all the houses. They had burnt some before, but on the 14th of April, it was the whole village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that they burnt all the houses but that they did not harm anyone in the village and that you fled from the village with your family to Djakovica. What actually happened? You said: "All the houses were burnt. They didn't harm anyone, and we escaped to Djakovica." Is that the essence of the story you're telling?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: It was only the person who was hit by a shell who was killed. Others, no. On the 25th of May, 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then you go on to say that you stayed in Djakovica until the end of March 1999. Is that correct, that you stayed there until the end of March 1999?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: We stayed there in Gjakove until 5th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Until the 5th of April. Does that mean, then, from May 1998 until the 5th of April, 1999 you were in Djakovica? Because that is what emerges from what you say, from what I'm asking you and from your answers. From May 1998 to the end of -- or, rather, the 5th of April, 1999, you were in Djakovica; right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you may be confusing the witness. The statement says: "25th of May --" I read this out -- "the Serbs started shelling the village. We continued to live in the village for two months more," and then you say: "but by that time, my family had already fled the village." Now, I may have missed this: When did you go to Gjakove?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We went in July, the beginning of July. I don't know the exact date, but it was in July 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you were there from July 1998 to the 5th of April, 1999. The witness --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. Mr. May, I think that cross-examination serves the purpose of having the witness answer orally to what it says here and not to prove whether something is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. written down or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but you mustn't mislead the witness, and you mustn't confuse her. The witness must have the chance of answering fairly and properly. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And do you think it's confusing for me to ask her whether that means from such-and-such a date, from May until April 1999, you were in Djakovica, that that is a confusing question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, it appears to me that every witness is a protected witness as far as you're concerned, different forms of protection, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is an improper comment. You know quite well why you get interrupted, and you will be interrupted if you try and confuse and mislead the witnesses. That is not a proper form of cross-examination and it's the Court's duty to stop it. Now, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this, please: In view of the fact that all the houses had been burnt, how were you able to go back to your father's house then?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: On 14th of April, 1999, all the houses were burnt. Let me say that again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But my question was this: As you say that that was the situation at the time, how were you able to go back to your father's house if it had been burnt? How could you return to a house that had been burnt down?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: On the 14th of April, 1999, when we set off for Albania, all the houses were burnt. They were burnt before, too, but on 14th of April, 1999, all the houses in Nivokaz were burnt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you answer me this: How did you go back to your father's house, how could you, if it had been burnt down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You will have to explain the question to the witness so that she can understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I mean what I'm asking, Mr. May. She says she went back to her father's house. Before that, she had claimed that all the houses had been burnt down. So I'm asking her now how she managed to return to her father's burnt-down house. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you understand the question? If you don't understand the question, Ms. Syla, simply say, "I don't understand the question," and the accused will have to clarify it. If you do understand the question, then answer it as best you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that on the 14th of April, 1999, all the houses were burnt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think he's asking you about earlier times. Mr. Milosevic, if you want this question clarified -- answered, you'll have to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you go back to your father's house?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: After the NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're talking about after the war. And during the war, when did you return to your father's house?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: During the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's try and clarify this. You go from the village to Gjakove in July of 1998. And then, as I understand it, on the 5th of April, you come back to the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you're there for a few days but then you're expelled. Is that the order of things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, I think the point that is being made is that on an earlier occasion, in July, I think you're saying that the Serbs burnt the houses, and I think all the houses, Judge Kwon kindly reminds me. Now, the point that's being made is if in July the Serbs had burnt all the houses, how were you able the following April to return to your father's house in the village? Do you understand the point that's being made? There may be an answer to it which you can give.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Right. Can you explain to us what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1998, in July, some houses were burnt. And on the 14th of April, 1999, all the houses were burnt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was your father's house one of the houses that were burnt in July 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the answer is it was not burnt; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: She just said that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You left Djakovica because of the bombing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: No; because of your police and army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you remember the bombing of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say -- can you tell us whether there was a mass bombing of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Only military targets. Only at weaponry. They didn't bomb the houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that at the time NATO targeted the very centre of town and that there was destruction and that a fire broke out? Do you remember that particular bombardment?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know the date. But I heard of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that on the occasion, 28 residential buildings were set fire to as a result of the explosions of the bombing in Djakovica? They went up in flames.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember that on the occasion, for example, Ferizi, Avni Ferizi and Shefqet Pruthi, in that bombing, the bombing in the centre of town, were killed? They were Albanians, both of them, and both from Djakovica. Do you remember how they were killed during that bombing? Do you remember how many casualties and victims remained under the debris after the bombing?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: The only victims were from the army and the police who entered the houses and executed people. That's what I've heard. Not from the bombing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But I understood you to say a moment ago that you had heard about these victims, the victims of the bombings of the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: She has given you the answer, and there's clearly a dispute about this as to who was responsible, and it's one we're going to have to resolve. Now, she wasn't there at the time, or she wasn't in the centre of town at the time, so she can only give very limited evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, Djakovica is not New York for somebody not to have been in the centre of town. If the centre of Djakovica is being bombarded, then there are no inhabitants of Djakovica who wouldn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In your statement, I see that you're quite well-versed in armaments, because in the 2001 statement, May, you say that the Yugoslav army was -- had automatic representatives of the Gulinov type. What kind of weaponry is that? Can you tell us? It's very specific, very specific weaponry. Could you explain it to us?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: I -- I only saw a few. I didn't see things with my own eyes. I just saw a few. I only saw automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And who told you to enumerate these weapons and to use their exact names, as you have done?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Can you ask the question, please? It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you the following: As you claim that they had the Gulinov type of automatic rifle, and you say that all you know is that it was automatic, so who told you that that was the name of that weapon and to say so, to state that? Because quite obviously you don't know that, it's not something that you yourself know; right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: I didn't talk about Gulinovs. I don't know what it is. I didn't talk about this in my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That is enough. What you say is quite sufficient. Now, tell me, if you were watching from a distance of 300 metres, were you able to recognise any type of weapon in particular?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Only when the city of Gjakove was burned we saw flames coming, and we saw the flames coming towards us. But we know that they didn't set fire to houses with Gulinovs but with some kind of small gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was after the bombing, wasn't it? You saw that flame after the bombing; right, the fire after the bombing?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: They began when the bombing began. The Serbs began acting when the bombing began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, did you ever have that kind of weapon in your hands? Did you hold a weapon of that type ever?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: I've never had an arm in my hands, an automatic weapon, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hold any kind of weapon in your hands?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, where is this reference that you're making to the Gulinov rifle? We can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's at page 2 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 2 of the statement --

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: -- of October --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- dated the 3rd of September 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Romano, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: It's on page 2 and the bottom of page 2 of the statement on the 5th of October, 2001, the second statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is this in the English?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes, in English. The seventh paragraph. The --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel. Microphone, please, Ms. Romano.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: "The attack started --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: That's the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement of the 5th of September, 2001, you also say that on the 6th of April, you started out from Djakovica on foot towards your village of Nivokaz and that there were 15 of you in the group, 15 people in the group. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that that was the first time you came to the village after you left it in 1998?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many people were there in the village at that time?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Quite a few when we returned to our village and the other villages too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were others there too. That means that the houses hadn't been burnt; right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: The other villages around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But your village wasn't burnt, just the villages around your own village; right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: All the villages were burnt down on the 14th of April, 1999; everything. There weren't any houses which were not unburnt [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, let's move on, not to waste time, because your statements are very interesting. How, then, can you explain the fact that in the village everything was burnt - that's what you say, right? - and that then you formed a column of 25 to 30 tractors with trailers and in each tractor there were over 20 people, et cetera. So how come this column started up? And if everything had been burnt, where did you get the tractors and the trailers from? Does that mean that the houses were burnt but not the tractors and trailers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let the witness answer. Can you deal with that, please? Were the tractors not burnt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the tractors were not burnt. In the village of Meja, Dobrosh, there were tractors which were not burnt. I didn't say that the tractors had all been burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That means, if I understand you -- or here's my question: Does that mean that the houses were burnt but that nobody touched the tractors? Right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you go on to say that the people loaded up their belongings onto the tractors. Now, if their houses had been burnt, where did they get their belongings from?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: All we put onto the tractors were the people, the family members. We didn't have any property to take with us. Also things from the unburnt houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, please, on 4 of your statement dated 2001, you say that the column of tractors was 15 kilometres long. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: It was about that. All the villages in the municipality of Gjakove were in that valley. So it was quite long. Dobrosh, Sheremetaj Dallashaj and Meja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if that was 15 kilometres, the head of the column was already in Djakovica, whereas the tail had not even left their yards in the surrounding villages yet. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: In Meja. It was a long convoy, about as long as I said, but it was very long. There were a lot of people in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me where you yourself were in that column; at the head of the column, at the end of the column, in the middle? Where were you?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: I was towards the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Towards the end of the column.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Not exactly at the end but towards the end. In the second half of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you able to assess that the column was 15 kilometres long if you were at its tail end, if you had joined it towards the end of the column?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Well, we waited for the first parts of the convoy to set off and to pass. We joined it towards the end. The other villages set off first. And we saw them passing, all the convoy as it passed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As you say that the police escorted you the whole time, does that mean that the policemen marched together with the convoy throughout its whole length, that is to say, 15 kilometres? How many policemen would there have been then?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: There were quite a few. You would know better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So that, then - let's just be specific - happened on the 14th of April, 1999. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your time is coming up. In fact, you've probably had the best part of three-quarters of an hour. So if you want to ask questions about what happened on the bridge, you should do so now. You have another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're speaking about the bridge at Bistrazin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're the one who's referring to it. Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you take a look at these photographs now, please. They show the bombed tractors, carbonised bodies, the people in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got the photos there? Yes. If the usher would get them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these the scenes?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There will be another one. The second one, please. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A group of people -- charred bodies, rather. Tell me, now, was this bombing by NATO?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: They -- a lot of people passed, and other planes passed afterwards. I don't know whether it was NATO or not. There was -- the army was there, and we were stopped and we were forced to get off the tractors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can we finish with those? Is there anything else you want to ask? Do you recognise that scene? Do you recognise that scene or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A lot of people hurt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, where were these three bombs thrown? Which part of the column? You say that there were three groups. Which part of the column was affected; the beginning, the end, the middle?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Ones at the beginning. I didn't see it, but I saw it at a distance, about 50 metres away, when the bombing from the plane came. And there were people hurt. There were 30 people on a tractor. It was a very small attack; when NATO attacked, the whole earth shook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand this right: Was the beginning of the column hit? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: The head of the convoy and towards the second half again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me. You were moving towards your houses; is that right? The column was moving towards their houses.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Can you ask that again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which direction was the column moving?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Towards Albania on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you said that it was a very long column, there were all tractors, many villagers on tractors - children, et cetera - was it visible from a great distance that this was a column of civilians? There were horse-drawn carts, too, in the column; right? There were children, there were civilians, old people.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you remember how many times aeroplanes bombed that column?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: In about seven places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, please, why did you state that you saw the Yugoslav air force signs on the aircraft? Who told you to say that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you to say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I saw the planes because they were very low. We could barely distinguish the NATO aircraft because they flew very high. If the NATO planes had -- the NATO planes were very, very high up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You claim that you saw with your very own eyes signs on the aeroplanes. Our very own signs on aeroplanes. Is that your assertion?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do these signs look like? What is it that you saw? Please describe for me what you saw.

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: The Yugoslav flag, a tricolour; red, white, and blue. This was the entire plan of the accused, to do this sort of thing and blame NATO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, fine. Now you finally revealed that. And do you know perhaps, if you ever listened to the radio, watched television, read newspapers, that NATO admitted that they had bombed that particular spot? They took the responsibility for that bombing and purportedly expressed their regrets over the fact that it had happened. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Perhaps NATO bombed at the beginning, but where we were, not our place, no. Nor for very long. It barely lasted for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be your last question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to give me an answer. Since you could not have seen Yugoslav aeroplanes and since it is well-known, generally known, who did this, who told you to state that it was Yugoslav aeroplanes that you had seen? Who told you to say that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: She has answered that question. She said nobody did, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and that is what she saw, and that's her evidence. No point arguing about it. Mr. Wladimiroff, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Romano.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Just one matter, Your Honour Re-examined by Ms. Romano:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, on the 25th of March, 1999, what happened to the centre of the town in the area of the old market?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: At night, when the NATO bombing started, the entire old market area of Gjakove was burnt, and they started to execute -- executing people. And we were to one side. We were in Cabrat. We could see things burning, and we could see them looting televisions and other appliance, and people told us that they were also executing people. And that was when they executed Dr. Izet Hima, the oldest doctor in Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, how far were you from the old centre, from the old town?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: We were on the edge of town, but the old market was quite close as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you --

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from this 200 metres, could you see who was doing the burning?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: We didn't see them that night, but we saw them the next day because they were burning houses at night -- during the day, too, and we saw them. They would fire at the houses and they would suddenly erupt into flames.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they police, soldiers?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: They were citizens and police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were they burning? Were they using any instrument, any weapon?

utterances.speaker: XHEVAHIRE SYLA
utterances.text: Guns. I don't know what they had in these guns, but they would fire at the houses and they would go up in flames.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Syla, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before the next witness is called, I think there is a matter that Mr. Wladimiroff wants to raise, and there are also a few matters I'm going to deal with first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: First of all, K32. We've considered the protective measures order and we'll grant it -- or the protective measures application; we'll grant it. Pseudonym and I think visual distortion, as I recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next matter is a ruling on the admissibility of the statement of Marjan Krasniqi under Rule 92 bis. The Trial Chamber will admit this statement under the Rule. It does not relate to the acts and conduct of the accused and is of a cumulative nature. It relates to incidents about which other evidence was given. The Trial Chamber will not require the witness to attend for cross-examination. The accused now says he wants to cross-examine the witness, but it was at his original request that the statement was exhibited. This request led to the application by the Prosecution. The accused did not consider cross-examination was necessary then when he made the application, and simply because the Prosecution have applied to have it admitted under 92 bis, there is no reason for cross-examination now. That said, it should be stressed that the Trial Chamber will take into consideration all the contents of the statement, and that includes the exculpatory parts. The original marking for the statement, which was Exhibit D23, will be vacated. That was a marking for identification. And it will be given a new exhibit number. If the registrar would do that, please. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 271.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His statement is contradictory to what was asserted. It is obvious from his statement that a local criminal group had committed the crime. The fact that I pointed out it's contradictory in nature cannot be a reason, to my mind, for this Prosecution witness not to be cross-examined here, although I pointed out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have ruled on that. You've heard me give the ruling. So there's no point arguing about it further. You also heard me say that we would take into account all the contents, including the exculpatory parts, and I remind you it was your application that the statement be exhibited. Now, we've taken all that into account and we've ruled. So it will be part of the evidence and you can refer to it. Now, Mr. Ryneveld, are we ready for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Wladimiroff, I'm sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. There is a matter I want to raise with the Court and that relates to the witness Karleusa, who will be on either today or tomorrow. Your Honours may have noticed that the filing related to this witness is confidential, and I'm not sure whether I should discuss the matter in open court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think there's going to be any application for confidentiality, protective measures, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right. I will try to deal with the matter as concisely as possible. The Court may remember there are attachments, annexes, to the intended statement of this witness. There are two newspaper articles, two communiques, that is, press releases, and a number of interviews conducted by the working group with about 21 or 22 witnesses, and a number of photographs. I have no difficulty with the photographs or the press communiques because I take it the accused will be able to cross-examine the witness on these issues. I do have a problem, though, with the newspaper articles. It seems not consistent with the policy of your Chamber to accept that opinions of journalists will be admitted as evidence. So we would object to that. Precisely I intend to explain to you why we have a difficulty with the number of interviews conducted with the working group. Your Honours may have noticed that these statements are -- not all of them are authenticated. There were some signatures on front pages but not really related to all the statements itself. So it seems to us that these are summaries by an investigator which are not under the -- well, let me rephrase it -- which should be not admitted by the Court if the Prosecutor intends to tender them. It's my understanding that the Prosecutor does intend to tender them. These statements would not qualify for a 92 bis statement because, as I said, these are not signed statements, nor will the Prosecutor -- nor will the accused be able to cross-examine these witnesses if they were tendered as 92 bis statements. So we believe it will not be fair to him to allow the witness -- to allow the Prosecution to have these statements tendered. Now, we can do two things: Either we can argue in detail when the witness will be here, or we will file a motion on the issue. It's up to the Court what you would prefer, I just want to alert you on the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, we've heard the objection. It would be much more convenient, I should have thought, to deal with it orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Prosecution are alerted to your objection, we are too, so we'll be able to consider it, and in due course we can hear full argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Very well, then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. In those circumstances, I propose to call Witness K32. And before he takes the courtroom, in light of your ruling for protective measures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's pointed out, Mr. Ryneveld, that it may be more convenient, in order that the Court could be prepared, if we take the adjournment now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, I was just about to say that. In light of protective measures, we're going to have to at least get him here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If we adjourn now for 20 minutes, we will be back at 20 to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, the first thing, could you put this paper in front of the witness, please. And there are copies of this document for Madam Registrar. Examined by Mr. Ryneveld:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, don't say anything yet. Just look at that piece of paper, and on that paper do you see your name and your date of birth and a number, K32, underneath it? Is that your name and birth date? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is the witness hearing translation? Does he have the right channel on?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. Can you hear me, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the piece of paper that you've just been given, sir. On it is a name and a date of birth, and underneath that, the number K32. Is that your name and date of birth? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I don't know whether we want to mark that as an exhibit. I believe we have in the past, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 272, to be kept under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do I understand, sir, that on the 26th of April of this year, 2002, you gave a statement to an investigator of the ICTY? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later on, sir, on the 8th of July, earlier this month, 2002, did you take another investigator, a Mr. Jonathan Sutch, on a tour of the area that you had discussed in that earlier statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in so doing, did you learn the names of some of the villages and locations which you were not familiar with at the time you gave your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Subsequently, sir, on the 15th of July of this year, two days ago, did you have an opportunity to review that earlier statement and make some corrections and amendments to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, sir, as a result of -- at my request, did you, with the assistance of members of the ICTY, produce or have produced a map which shows the areas to which you will be making reference in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps -- we have copies, colour copies of that document. Perhaps that can be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just looking very briefly at that map, if you would, please, sir, does that map show -- the little green circles on the map, does that show the areas that you've made reference to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes. It shows everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might that be marked as an exhibit at this point and then we can refer to it as he goes through his evidence, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 273.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness K32, I understand, sir, that you are 26 years old, you're a Muslim, and you're from Montenegro; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, that you were conscripted to start your service with the VJ in March of 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then by the 10th of June of 1998, I understand that you were sent to Prizren in Kosovo, and you joined the Logistics Corps as a driver. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after some time, you eventually ended up being assigned to a combat group in the village of Damjane which was, at the time, occupied by civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell us from your knowledge as a driver in the area, did you visit -- what was your function as a driver? What were you specifically doing? Where were you driving to and what were you delivering?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: I was driving food in the army. I was delivering food throughout the field. And water too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do I understand correctly, sir, that there were various combat groups in the area where you had to deliver your food and water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it the translation I didn't get was, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, how many combat groups were there in the area, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these five combat groups, do you happen to know who their commander was? Who was in charge of these five groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Colonel Bozidar Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And under him, did each of those combat groups have a particular commander in charge of each individual group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about in your group? Who was the commander of your particular combat group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Mostly they were lieutenant colonels by rank, and Bozidar was in command of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "Bozidar," you're talking about Delic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, what combat group were you in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Combat group 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many soldiers were in your combat group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: There were between 150 to 190 soldiers. It differed and changed. From 150 to 190.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your particular combat group, are you aware whether it had any military equipment of any kind, and if so, very briefly, what kind of equipment was at its disposal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes, it did: Two tanks, four howitzers, and a number of military vehicles for transporting the soldiers and for the purposes of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, shortly after -- you've told us that you were moved to Damjane. Once you got to Damjane, did something happen? Did you see Colonel Delic arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upon his arrival, are you aware of what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of it. Upon his arrival, he issued orders to the officers subordinate to him, and he said that they should get all the civilians out of the houses, that there should be no civilians left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how is it that you know about that order? Did you hear it personally or did you hear it from someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: I didn't hear it personally, but the soldier who was with me told me about it, and he heard him say that personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In any event, what did the soldiers do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: The soldiers, following orders issued by their commanders, went from house to house and ordered the people to come out of the houses, the civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened -- like, how quickly did the civilians in Damjane, how quickly did they follow the order to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Well, the order was that they should leave within the day. And actually, they left within the space of three hours -- or, rather, 3.00. It was 3.00 when everybody had left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember about what time of day they were told to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: In the course of the day by noon. We came in the morning. As fast as possible, that they should leave as fast as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, by the following day, were there any civilians left in Damjane, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: No, there were none left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, did the civilians take with them or leave behind upon having been told by your fellow soldiers to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: They only took their personal belongings with them and left all the rest. The army said that they wouldn't touch any of their property, that they could feel free to leave it behind. So they only took their personal belongings with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any vehicles left behind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes, the vehicles were left behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to those vehicles once the civilians left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: We took them. The Yugoslav army took them for army purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the army live up to its promise to these civilians that they would not touch their personal belongings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Well, what they told the civilians they didn't abide by. They told them that they wouldn't touch their property and that they wouldn't touch their houses, but they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, once these civilians left, what steps were taken to -- were any steps taken at all in order to secure the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: First of all, we blocked the roads. We put up barriers on the roads, and nobody could enter the village after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did anyone try?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: They did try, some people, but they weren't allowed to enter. They came back to take some more belongings, but they weren't allowed in. The army didn't permit them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to them, if anything, when they did try to get into the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: They were mistreated somewhat by the soldiers, and similar things, and so they had to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you earlier told us, sir, about the army not living up to its promise not to touch their belongings. Do you know anything about what happened to the contents of a house or houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Most of the things were taken away, like television sets, radios, and all that kind of electrical equipment and other things from the house, and some of the officers would take them to their own homes. I saw that taking place personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they leave their cattle behind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They left their cattle behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the cattle or any of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Well, mostly the sheep. How can I put it? They took the sheep for themselves to eat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the soldiers live while in Damjane?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: In the houses, the civilian houses, the ones we had expelled the people from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. I'm going to turn you next, your mind next, if I may, to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the period between the 1st and the 3rd of August of 1998. Were you aware of what was known as a mopping-up operation between those dates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: I did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall an instance of an area between Djakovica, along the road to Klina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Sir, what happened on the road between Djakovica towards Klina between the 1st and the 3rd of August? Can you tell us a little bit of background about how it was that you were on that road and what you were doing and what happened, if a specific instance happened, while you were doing that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: There was a very large army column going to help the police as reinforcement. We were going as reinforcements. The first village we came to, we stopped. Colonel Bozidar Delic ordered a tanker -- tankist to turn the tank around towards a house, and that was at the first village we had arrived at, and ordered him to fire at the house. I saw and heard that personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We're going to get to that in just a moment. I'm going to back you up just a little bit first.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm at paragraph 6 of the summary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: En route towards this village that you referred to, do you recall an instance where you were delivering water to some soldiers and that there had been an incident in a cornfield?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about that first, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: When I was delivering water to the soldiers, some of the soldiers - and I had quite a lot of friends there - I saw two dead people, Albanians, five or six metres away from me, and I asked one of my friends what had happened, and he said, "We found them alive in the cornfields over there, and we asked them some things and then we killed them."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you look at the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice anything about any kind of wounds to these bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that the bodies had no ears, and in the nape of the neck, that's where they were shot at with pistols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell whether this had been a recent killing or whether that had happened quite some time ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes. The killing had taken place just before I had arrived, not long before. Perhaps half an hour. Half an hour. They were killed half an hour before I had arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to why your friends or the soldiers killed these two men? Were you told anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Allegedly, those two Albanians told them that there was a trench of some kind up there of 200 metres and that there were more people up there who were armed. But I didn't believe that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And upon telling the soldiers that information, they were killed? Is that what you understood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right. Straight away. The soldier who saw it take place told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you informed whether there had been any kind of a gun battle leading up to this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: I didn't learn of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, sir, I understand that you were there when a coroner's van arrived and took the bodies away; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were about to tell us, before I asked you to back up and tell us about this incident, about Colonel Delic stopping outside a village and telling a tank to do something. First of all, do you have -- do you know approximately where that village was and do you now know the name of the village? Perhaps you might want to look at the map, if the exhibit is available to the witness. Do you see the map there? The left margin.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the name of the village of this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Medevce, the village of Medevce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that spelled M-e-c-e/M-e-q-e depending on whether it's Serbian or Albanian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a "D" I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Perhaps I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm just looking at the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was written up in Albanian and in Serbian, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps you could point --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: There are two, yes, Your Honours. I see there is also a Medevce in the middle of the map and then there's a Mece in the extreme left top quadrant of the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which village are you speaking about now, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps we could show it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This one here. Here it is, I've already indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, the witness does appear to be pointing to the green circle in the top left quadrant of the map, which is Mece.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened there, sir, when you got to that village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: We stopped at a spot. The village was about 300 metres away from us. Bozidar Delic got out of his car, he ordered us to stop, all of us. He came up to the tank, and he waited a few minutes and then ordered him to fire a shell at the house that could be seen over there, which the tank did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: Nothing happened. But then he waited for a few more minutes and then gave the same order, that another shell should be fired. And then the civilians, mostly women and children, started fleeing from the house and fleeing towards the woods behind the houses. And then he ordered the infantry to start out towards the houses there and to start their operation. That's what I heard him order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "start their operation," did he tell them what to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: To start the mop-up operation. That's understood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you understand that order to mean to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K32
utterances.text: I understood it to mean that the terrorists should be killed and -- well, I didn't understand whether it applied to civilians too, but anyway, he ordered them to start mopping up. But they didn't tell us anything, no concrete -- nothing in specific terms.
